newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's slain army chief helped quell rebellions.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's slain army chief helped quell rebellions.

text.p: General Mahele Lieko Bokungo, Zaire's army chief killed by the presidential guard on Friday, had popped up on repeated occasions since President Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in 1965 to help quell internal rebellions.
He was named Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister in Mobutu's National Salvation Government formed in April.

But he apparently saw the writing on the wall for Mobutu because he was supposed to meet rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Saturday in the Zambian capital Lusaka to discuss the transition of power, according to a reliable diplomatic source.

An experienced and respected officer trained in France and Israel and by Zaire's former colonial rulers Belgium, Mahele had been granted unprecedented powers to control the hitherto untouchable presidential guard.

Mobutu returned from a prolonged absence in Europe in December and the next day named Mahele to take command of the Zairean Armed Forces, which had been sent reeling by Kabila's Tutsi-led revolt in the east.

Mobutu fired Mahele from the same post in 1993 and military sources say the general gave stiff conditions before taking up the army command again. These included powers to sanction senior officers and total control over the armed forces including the elite presidential guard, until then answerable to Mobutu alone.
Before his appointment, political leaders, local newspapers and regular soldiers battling Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsis all called for him to take command.
Some sources say Mahele had the blessing of France, which had troops stationed in Africa and intervened in the past to help Mobutu.

Mahele was respected among rank and file soldiers and had a reputation for discipline and military skill among the wider population, making him the obvious choice to boost troop morale and restore public confidence in the ragged Zairean army.
He was one of the rare group of top generals in Zaire who earned their senior ranking on the battlefield and not through close family ties with Mobutu.
Born in 1941, Mahele was recruited into the army the year Mobutu took over power in a military coup d'etat, in 1965.
"Mahele is a trained carpenter who became a fervent Jehovah's Witness, going from door to door to spread his message," one Zaire watcher wrote in 1991.
He came from the Mbuza tribe which is close to Mobutu's Gbandi. On many occasions in Zaire's turbulent post-independence history, he played a role in suppressing internal rebellion.
He was Mobutu's chief bodyguard for several years from 1969 and avoided a reputation for corruption or lavish living that some of Mobutu's closer generals attracted.
Eleven years ago he fought back Kabila, who had set up a rebel republic on the shores of Lake Tanganyika around the town of Moba.

He also had experience fighting Tutsi rebels in Rwanda when he led Zairean soldiers in 1990 to back up the Hutu government of the late president Juvenal Habyarimana. But the Tutsi rebels went on to seize power in 1994 and are supporting the present revolt in Zaire.

In 1991 Mahele became chief of staff of the armed forces and was widely credited with putting down a round of army-led looting in the capital Kinshasa when he gave orders for loyal troops to fire on looters in 1993.

But when he criticised the army's role in Zaire before a national conference that year, and called for reforms, he was removed from the position and subsequently kept a low profile as military adviser to the president.
